title: Bhuman — the infinite, where one sees nothing else (7.23–7.24)
hook: at the top of the ladder Sanatkumara says it plainly: there's no happiness in the small; the infinite is happiness
tomorrow: the city of Brahman in the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: meditation, then understanding, strength, food and water, a ladder asking what holds each thing up. Your line was the ladder climbs.

A kid swimming far out on a summer afternoon. Friends at a table late at night, laughing until it hurts. A parent holding a newborn at 3am. Some people say afterward that in moments like these there was no thought of being happy. No one over here, and happiness over there. Just the thing itself. Sanatkumara's ladder, after many rungs, arrives at something like that, and gives it a name.
screen: `NO THOUGHT OF BEING HAPPY.` → `NO ONE OVER HERE.` → `JUST THE THING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Between yesterday and today, the ladder climbs through heat, space, memory, hope and breath, then turns toward truth, understanding, thinking, faith, steadfastness and action. At the top, Sanatkumara says: a person acts only when they find happiness. So, Narada, you should want to understand happiness. Then the line at the heart of the chapter. Yo vai bhuma tat sukham, nalpe sukham asti. The infinite is happiness. There is no happiness in the small. Bhuma means the vast, the full, the unbounded. Alpa means the small, the limited. Here's how to tell them apart: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else, that is the infinite. Where one sees, hears, understands something else, that is the small. Think back to the ocean, the laughter, the newborn: nothing else, for a moment. A taste of what he means. Narada asks: but sir, what does the infinite rest on? On its own greatness, Sanatkumara says. Or, not even on greatness. People here call cows and horses greatness, and elephants and gold, servants and spouses, fields and houses. I don't mean that. Those things rest on something else. The infinite rests on nothing. It's above and below, east and west, everywhere. And then: I am all this. The self is all this. The chapter ends quietly: Sanatkumara showed Narada the far shore beyond darkness.
screen: `WE ACT TO FIND HAPPINESS.` · `NO HAPPINESS IN THE SMALL.` · `WHERE ONE SEES NOTHING ELSE.` · `NOT COWS, GOLD OR HOUSES.` · then, large: `YO VAI BHUMA TAT SUKHAM.`

segments.voice: Let your attention spread, the sounds in the room, then beyond it, then as far as you can hear, and let your sense of space open above, below and on every side. When a thought pulls you into something small, notice it, and let the space open again.
Bhuman. The infinite, the vast: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else. There's no happiness in the small.
Your line: the infinite is happiness. Yo vai bhuma tat sukham, the line at the heart. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote 'the infinite is happiness; there is no happiness in the small' when distinguishing lasting joy from pleasure in possessions, and the bhuma-vidya is a standard topic in Vedanta study.

match.prompt: the infinite and the small — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: you're Narada. Sanatkumara has said the infinite is happiness. you ask what the infinite rests on. what does he answer?
options: on its own greatness, or not even on greatness.
on cows, gold and good houses.
fork.reveal: it rests on nothing else. the things people call greatness rest on something; the infinite is everywhere.

original.note: Sanskrit bhūmā (stem bhūman): the vast, the infinite, fullness. yo vai bhūmā tat sukham.

trapdoor: what you thought: think big, be happy.
what it means: lasting happiness is the infinite, where there's nothing else; anything with an outside is small and passes.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 7.23–7.24, the bhuma-vidya; the Brahma Sutras (1.3.8) discuss whether bhuma here means prana or Brahman.

chat.says: What does Sanatkumara say real happiness is?
options: The infinite: where you see nothing else. There's no happiness in the small.
Having plenty: cows, gold, fields and houses, the greatness people call it.
Getting what you want, one wish at a time, until there's nothing left to want.
chat.meaning: Yo vai bhuma tat sukham: the infinite is happiness; there is none in the small. The infinite is where one sees nothing else.

Narada.meaning: a famous sage, learned in every subject of his day
